# Googlebot

*Crawler*

Google Search's main crawler, which fetches pages for the index as a smartphone or desktop user agent.

Narrative: the topic [The crawl pipeline](../topics/crawl-pipeline.md) tells the story; this card lists what links to it.

68 claims mention it: 13 from Google's documentation, 43 shown or said at the event (5 not in Google docs, 8 confirmed by Google docs, 22 consistent with Google docs, 8 nothing to verify), 12 the author's analysis. A card is a map: cite the claim ids, with the citation given after each claim.

## Google's documentation

Documented in: [Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/overview-google-crawlers), [List of Google's common crawlers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers), [Verify requests from Google crawlers and fetchers](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/verify-google-requests), [Inside Googlebot: demystifying crawling, fetching, and the bytes we process](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post).

- [`D1-C136`](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) Docs: Google's Inside Googlebot post (March 2026) says Googlebot currently fetches only the first 2MB of each URL, HTTP headers included (64MB for PDFs); bytes past that cutoff are not fetched, rendered or indexed, and each resource the page loads has its own separate limit. `[D1-C136, docs, Search Central blog (31 March 2026), https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post]`
- [`D1-C137`](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) Docs: Google's Inside Googlebot post warns that bloated inline base64 images, large blocks of inline CSS or JavaScript, or megabytes of menus can push a page's text or structured data past Googlebot's 2MB cutoff, and advises moving heavy CSS and JavaScript to external files and placing meta tags, the title, the canonical and essential structured data high in the HTML. `[D1-C137, docs, Search Central blog (31 March 2026), https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post]`
- [`D1-C342`](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) Docs: Google's Inside Googlebot post (March 2026) says Googlebot is today just one user of a centralized crawling platform, and that dozens of other clients, such as Google Shopping and AdSense, send their crawl requests through the same infrastructure under other crawler names, with only the larger ones documented. `[D1-C342, docs, Search Central blog (31 March 2026), https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/03/crawler-blog-post]`
- [`D1-C138`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Docs: Google's page on verifying its crawlers says Googlebot and Google's other common crawlers resolve to crawl-*.googlebot.com or geo-crawl-*.geo.googlebot.com host names, special-case crawlers to rate-limited-proxy-*.google.com and user-triggered fetchers to *.gae.googleusercontent.com or google-proxy-*.google.com, and it publishes each group's IP ranges as JSON files such as common-crawlers.json and special-crawlers.json. `[D1-C138, docs, Google, https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/verify-google-requests]`
- [`D1-C141`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Docs: Google's guide to A/B testing says never to show one set of URLs to Googlebot and a different set to humans: that is cloaking, which is against Google's spam policies whether or not a test is running. `[D1-C141, docs, Google Search Central, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/website-testing]`
- [`D2-C095`](../sessions/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) Docs: Google's Search documentation gives notranslate as a rule for a robots or googlebot meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag header, and says the rule opts a page out of all translation features in Google Search. `[D2-C095, docs, Google Search Central, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/translated-results]`
- [`D2-C101`](../sessions/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) Docs: Google's robots meta tag specification says Googlebot considerably decreases the crawl rate of a URL after the date and time set in its unavailable_after rule. `[D2-C101, docs, Google Search Central, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag]`
- [`D2-C131`](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) Docs: Google's JavaScript SEO guide says Googlebot sends every page with a 200 HTTP status code to the rendering queue, whether or not it contains JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header tells Google not to index it, and Google uses the rendered HTML to index the page. `[D2-C131, docs, Google Search Central, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics]`
- [`D2-C164`](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) Docs: Google says Googlebot and its Web Rendering Service identify resources that do not contribute to essential page content, such as reporting and error requests, and may not fetch them, so client-side analytics may not give a full or accurate picture of their activity. `[D2-C164, docs, Google Search Central, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript]`
- [`D2-C169`](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) Docs: Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says Googlebot extracts links twice, from the HTML response before rendering and again from the rendered HTML, so links injected with JavaScript can be found if they use crawlable `<a href>` markup. `[D2-C169, docs, Google Search Central, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics]`
- [`D2-C206`](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) Docs: Google says its Web Rendering Service fetches the resources a page references through Googlebot, including JavaScript, CSS and XHR requests to APIs, but not images or videos. `[D2-C206, docs, Search Central blog (3 December 2024), Search Central blog (31 March 2026), https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2024/12/crawling-december-resources]`
- [`D2-C278`](../sessions/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) Docs: For effects that need WebGL, which Googlebot does not support, Google's guide to fixing JavaScript problems suggests skipping the effect or prerendering it with server-side rendering so that the content is accessible to Googlebot. `[D2-C278, docs, Google Search Central, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/fix-search-javascript]`
- [`D2-C561`](../sessions/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) Docs: Google's documentation says Googlebot mostly crawls from US IP addresses and sends no Accept-Language header, so pages that change content or redirect by the visitor's perceived country or language may not have every version crawled, indexed or ranked; it recommends separate URLs annotated with hreflang. `[D2-C561, docs, Google Search Central, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/locale-adaptive-pages]`

## Shown or said at the event

Not in Google's documentation first: present those as said at Search Central Live, never as documented policy.

- [`D1-C123`](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) Slide, Day 1, not in Google docs: Bing closes the robots.txt group at an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines, so in the slide's example bingbot ends up not blocked while Googlebot is; the slide warned that different crawlers behave differently. `[D1-C123, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C536`](../sessions/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) Stage, Day 1, not in Google docs: Dave Smart said this applies to all redirects, not only JavaScript ones; his examples: a redirect through an external authorisation service that is blocked by its own robots.txt, content that moved through several URLs over the years with one of them later blocked, and unexpected redirects, such as one served only to Googlebot's user agent. `[D1-C536, stage, Dave Smart, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C467`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, not in Google docs: To check that new content is crawled fast enough, Gary Illyes advised measuring the time between publishing a URL and Googlebot's first crawl of it: ideally it stays flat or falls, and only a rising trend calls for investigation. `[D1-C467, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C543`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, not in Google docs: Gary Illyes said that if the time from publishing to Googlebot's first crawl starts rising, how much it rises matters: for the crawling of fresh stories, something like two hours is probably not great (a smaller example figure is unclear in the recording). `[D1-C543, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 1]`
- [`D3-C108`](../sessions/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) Stage, Day 3, not in Google docs: A community speaker compared Googlebot to an inspector who cannot enter the shop and only looks through the window, seeing the page as ones and zeros, which the speaker linked to tokenization. `[D3-C108, stage, a community speaker, Day 3]`
- [`D1-C203`](../sessions/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) Stage, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: A crawler is software that downloads pages, extracts their links and repeats the process on the links it extracted; Googlebot is the main crawler of Google Search. `[D1-C203, stage, Cherry Prommawin, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C087`](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) Slide, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: Googlebot ignores an unknown line, such as a Content-signal line, placed between two user-agent lines and joins both user agents into one group, so the rules that follow apply to both; in the slide's example both are blocked. `[D1-C087, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C533`](../sessions/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) Stage, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: Dave Smart said robots.txt groups are not additive: if a group matches a crawler's user agent, only that group's rules apply, so a googlebot group that blocks /dogs/ leaves Googlebot free to crawl the /goats/ and /cows/ that the * group blocks. `[D1-C533, stage, Dave Smart, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C108`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Slide, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: The non-standard crawl-delay rule is not processed by Googlebot, so it does not save any crawl budget. `[D1-C108, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C375`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Stage, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: Googlebot as a single standalone crawler is a historical idea: Google crawls through a centralised crawling infrastructure, so a request from a Google user agent in server logs is a request routed through that shared platform. `[D1-C375, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C491`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: If paginated pages are replaced by a load-more button or infinite scroll without crawlable links to them, Google will not see the further pages at all. `[D1-C491, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D2-C057`](../sessions/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) Slide, Day 2, confirmed by Google docs: The robots meta tag is written as `<meta name="robots" content="rule1,rule2">`, or with the name googlebot instead of robots, with several rules separated by commas. `[D2-C057, slide, John Mueller, Day 2]`
- [`D3-C387`](../sessions/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) Stage, Day 3, confirmed by Google docs: Storebot-Google also does deep crawls, for example of checkout pages, which do not belong in the search index; this is another reason it is kept separate from Googlebot. `[D3-C387, stage, Alex Jansen, Day 3]`
- [`D1-C037`](../sessions/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) Slide, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: For classic Search, crawling means Googlebot, scheduling and robots.txt, with AI used in parts such as scheduling. Indexing is one big but not limitless index that calculates signals and understands more than words, with AI such as BERT. Serving uses hundreds of signals tailored to the moment, with AI such as RankBrain. `[D1-C037, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C322`](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Googlebot is an ordinary HTTP client with nothing special about it: like a browser, it fetches a URL it was given and returns the fetched bytes to Google's servers. `[D1-C322, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C325`](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Googlebot is the crawler Google uses for web search, including Search's AI features. `[D1-C325, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C366`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Google treats a 402 Payment Required response as a 404 Not Found, because Googlebot cannot pay for content. `[D1-C366, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C367`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: CDN captcha challenges often return HTTP 200; Googlebot does not solve them and sees only content with a 200 status, which indexing then classifies as a soft 404, reported as an error in Search Console. `[D1-C367, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C519`](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: A user-agent line with its allow and disallow rules forms a user-agent group, and one group can name several crawlers (the talk's example: Googlebot and Bingbot); give named crawlers their own group only when they need rules the * group should not grant to every crawler. `[D1-C519, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C531`](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: In the talk's quiz, the answer for letting Googlebot crawl /staging/preview/ while keeping the rest of /staging/ closed to it was a user-agent: googlebot group with both rules, disallow /staging/ and allow /staging/preview/, rather than an allow in the * group or a Googlebot group with only the allow. `[D1-C531, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C443`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: To judge crawl efficiency, check Search Console's Crawl Stats report: whether total crawling has plateaued over time, and whether the average response time shows the server is fast enough or is limiting Googlebot. `[D1-C443, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C469`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Gary Illyes said disallowing a section that should not be crawled, such as /ads, in a Googlebot group in robots.txt shifts crawl budget to the rest of the site. `[D1-C469, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C473`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Files such as cats.txt have no importance for Google Search: if a site links to one, Googlebot will find and crawl it, but it has no other effect. `[D1-C473, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C494`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: To check whether Google lowered a site's crawl capacity limit, look at the number of connections Googlebot opens to the site: if it has dropped, the capacity limit changed. `[D1-C494, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C114`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: A Google panelist called pagination one of the trickiest things in web development and said switching to infinite scroll or a load-more button is risky, depending on what you want to achieve, because Googlebot does not click buttons. `[D1-C114, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C546`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: A Google panelist illustrated a crawl capacity limit drop as a step down in the site's hostload, for example from 10 to 5, which the panelist said means Googlebot then makes up to five requests per second (the recording adds 'per connection', which is unclear). `[D1-C546, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C075`](../sessions/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Googlebot does not support HTTP/3 today. `[D1-C075, stage, a speaker, Day 1]`
- [`D2-C040`](../sessions/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) Slide, Day 2, consistent with Google docs: Google cannot extract a link from an a element that only has an onclick handler, because Googlebot does not click, so the JavaScript is never triggered. `[D2-C040, slide, Google, Day 2]`
- [`D2-C197`](../sessions/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) Slide, Day 2, consistent with Google docs: Lazy loading triggered by a scroll event listener, such as window.addEventListener('scroll', loadMoreProducts), never runs for Googlebot because Googlebot does not scroll. `[D2-C197, slide, Rebecca Yu, Day 2]`
- [`D2-C266`](../sessions/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) Slide, Day 2, consistent with Google docs: Google named three causes of content missing from the rendered HTML: JavaScript inaccessible to Googlebot, JavaScript DOM event triggers and disabled browser APIs. `[D2-C266, slide, Erin Sparling, Day 2]`
- [`D2-C267`](../sessions/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) Stage, Day 2, consistent with Google docs: When the JavaScript is not accessible to Googlebot, Google cannot render the client-side DOM that the page builds asynchronously, so parts of the page may be present while the main content is absent. `[D2-C267, stage, Erin Sparling, Day 2]`
- [`D2-C374`](../sessions/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) Stage, Day 2, consistent with Google docs: A growing cause of wrong clustering is bot protection: when a CDN or another protection system shows Googlebot the same 'you look like a bot, solve this puzzle' page on many unrelated URLs or domains, Google can cluster those pages as duplicates. `[D2-C374, stage, Google, Day 2]`
- [`D2-C375`](../sessions/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) Stage, Day 2, consistent with Google docs: Google's systems find it very hard to recognise a bot-challenge page as an error page, and Googlebot cannot solve the puzzles, such as selecting all the cats, that those pages ask for. `[D2-C375, stage, Google, Day 2]`
- [`D3-C116`](../sessions/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) Stage, Day 3, consistent with Google docs: Google's long-standing advice to write for people and give them what they want has become true in practice because Googlebot has become more and more human, a community speaker argued. `[D3-C116, stage, a community speaker, Day 3]`
- [`D3-C385`](../sessions/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) Stage, Day 3, consistent with Google docs: Google Shopping uses its own crawler, Storebot (Storebot-Google), instead of Googlebot because it needs fresh product information, prices, availability and shipping details and therefore crawls much more often. `[D3-C385, stage, Alex Jansen, Day 3]`
- [`D1-C079`](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) Slide, Day 1, nothing to verify: The robots.txt session worked through an example file with three groups: a default group that disallows everything except the bare homepage, a shared bingbot and googlebot group that also allows /politics/ and /*/live/, and a google-extended group that disallows /subscriptions/. `[D1-C079, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C387`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Stage, Day 1, nothing to verify: An audience member asked, in questions submitted before the event, how often Googlebot should be expected to visit a site now that AI Mode has rolled out, and whether AI means more crawling. `[D1-C387, stage, an audience member, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C481`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, nothing to verify: An audience member asked whether Google plans dedicated user agents for AI, as OpenAI has several, so that site owners can control AI access separately from Googlebot and analyse it in their logs. `[D1-C481, stage, an audience member, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C484`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, nothing to verify: A Google panelist called blocking all AI crawlers while allowing search crawlers such as Googlebot, Bingbot and Applebot a personal, philosophical decision that every site owner can make. `[D1-C484, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D2-C001`](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) Slide, Day 2, nothing to verify: An audience member asked whether HTML sitemaps still matter for large sites, whether they improve Googlebot's crawl discovery and whether they pass link equity to deeper pages. `[D2-C001, slide, an audience member, Day 2]`
- [`D2-C839`](../sessions/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) Stage, Day 2, nothing to verify: An audience member asked how several sloppy migrations on the same domain can affect Googlebot's crawling. `[D2-C839, stage, an audience member, Day 2]`
- [`D3-C097`](../sessions/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) Stage, Day 3, nothing to verify: In Lightning session K (Facets of quality), a community speaker argued that SEO is for humans: write for people and the problems they have, rather than to please Googlebot. `[D3-C097, stage, a community speaker, Day 3]`
- [`D3-C107`](../sessions/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) Stage, Day 3, nothing to verify: Because Googlebot is not a human, the speaker's team at the time thought more about Googlebot than about human readers, a community speaker said. `[D3-C107, stage, a community speaker, Day 3]`

## The author's analysis

- [`D1-C344`](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) Analysis: On stage Google spoke of probably hundreds, if not thousands, of crawlers, while its Inside Googlebot post speaks of dozens of other clients; both agree that only the larger crawlers are documented, so a Google user agent missing from the public lists is not proof of a fake request, and reverse DNS or Google's published IP ranges are the test. `[D1-C344, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D1-C078`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Analysis: For temporary blocks return 503 or 429, never a 200 page with a captcha or error message, which becomes a soft 404 and can replace real content in the index. Verify Googlebot by reverse DNS, not by user agent. `[D1-C078, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D1-C372`](../sessions/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) Analysis: Do not answer verified Googlebot with 401, 402 or 403, for example from a login wall, a paywall or a pay-per-crawl setup: Google treats them like 404 and drops the pages, and Google's status code page says not to use 401 or 403 to limit crawling; to slow crawling temporarily, return 429 or 503. `[D1-C372, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D1-C083`](../sessions/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) Analysis: Under the example file, Googlebot may crawl /, /politics/eu-vote and /sports/live/, and is blocked from /?utm_source=x, /index.html, /politics (no trailing slash), /live/ and /sports/live-score. An 'allow: /$' rule does not cover the homepage with tracking parameters. `[D1-C083, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D1-C419`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Analysis: A 404 fetch is still a fetch: Google's 2017 crawl budget post says generally any URL Googlebot crawls counts towards a site's crawl budget, so the stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget is best read as 'they do not slow crawling, and a 404 tells Google to crawl that URL less over time'. `[D1-C419, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D1-C486`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Analysis: The panel spoke of blocking Google's 'AI crawling or training' with Google-Extended, but Google documents Google-Extended as a usage token, not a crawler: disallowing it does not stop Googlebot fetching pages and only controls use for Gemini training and grounding. `[D1-C486, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D1-C547`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Analysis: Google's crawl budget guide does not express the crawl capacity limit in requests per second: it limits the total time a server spends holding connections open for Google, counting both the number of parallel connections and their duration. That fits the panel's advice to watch how many connections Googlebot opens (D1-C494): fewer connections is the documented form of a lower capacity limit. `[D1-C547, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D2-C098`](../sessions/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) Analysis: International sites should remove notranslate from their templates unless translation must be prevented: the robots or googlebot form switches off Google Search's translation features, and John Mueller said the form named google also blocks Chrome's translation for visitors who do not read the language. `[D2-C098, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D2-C378`](../sessions/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) Analysis: Check what your CDN or bot protection serves to verified Googlebot and to the AI agents you want to allow; if crawlers must get a challenge page, return it with a 503 status as Google recommends, never as a 200 page across many URLs, which Google may cluster as duplicates. `[D2-C378, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D3-C109`](../sessions/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) Analysis: The inspector metaphor blends two steps: Googlebot fetches pages during crawling, while tokenization happens later when the page is processed for the index, as Google explained on Day 2. `[D3-C109, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D3-C301`](../sessions/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) Analysis: For developers, Google's five listed spam types map to concrete checks: serve Googlebot the same content as users (cloaking), avoid near-identical location or keyword pages (doorways), add value to reused content (scraped content), and patch and monitor the CMS against injected pages and links (hacked content). `[D3-C301, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D3-C390`](../sessions/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) Analysis: Treat Storebot-Google separately from Googlebot in robots.txt and bot protection: a shop that blocks it on product, cart or checkout paths can undermine Shopping price and availability checks, even when Googlebot is allowed. `[D3-C390, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`

## For developers

- `DEV-CAN-11` **AVOID** · Documented: Never route a crawlable URL's redirects through a URL that robots.txt blocks (1 of its claims mentions it; its own text names it)
- `DEV-IDX-08` **MAY** · Documented: Use unavailable_after on pages with a known end date (1 of its claims mentions it; its own text names it)
- `DEV-IDX-09` **SHOULD** · Documented: Leave notranslate and noimageindex out of templates unless translation or image indexing must be prevented (2 of its claims mention it; its own text names it)
- `DEV-INT-01` **MUST** · Documented: Give every language and country version its own URL (1 of its claims mentions it; its own text names it)
- `DEV-INT-02` **AVOID** · Documented: Do not redirect visitors automatically by IP address or browser language (1 of its claims mentions it; its own text names it)
